title: Stagger Screens
description: Two screens set in a line, one after another — double trouble for the shooter's defender.
whatIsIt: A stagger is two off-ball screens set in a line — one behind the other — for the same cutter. The shooter's defender has to fight through two screens in about two seconds, which is nearly impossible to do cleanly.

Staggers are usually run for shooters coming from the baseline to the wing or top: pin down, then a second pin down right behind it. The double screen is the point — one screen is navigable, two in sequence usually aren't.
It's a staple of every serious offense because it's simple to teach and brutally effective. Two screeners, one shooter, one open jumper.
whyItMatters: One screen can be fought through; two screens in a stagger force the defense to choose between switching (mismatch), trailing (late contest), or going under (open shot). Every option favors the offense.

howTo.title: Line up the two screeners
howTo.detail: Set the screens in a vertical line with a step or two between them — both legal, both set before the cutter arrives.

howTo.title: Shooter: sprint the gauntlet
howTo.detail: Come off the first screen shoulder-to-shoulder, then immediately the second. Don't slow down between them — the speed is what breaks the defender.

howTo.title: Read after the second screen
howTo.detail: Curl if the defender trails, flare if they cheat, straight for the jumper if they go under. The read comes after screen two.

howTo.title: Screeners: hold both
howTo.detail: Both screens must be held through contact. If the first screener releases early, the defender slips through and the stagger collapses.

howTo.title: Time the pass
howTo.detail: The passer throws as the shooter clears the second screen — not before, not after. Late passes get contested.

coachingPoints: Spacing between the screens matters — too close and it's one screen, too far and the defender recovers between them.
Drill both screeners' timing: the second must be set before the cutter arrives.
Teach the shooter to read, not to run a route — the defender's reaction decides the finish.
Practice vs a switching defense too; staggers create switches that must be exploited.
commonMistakes: Screens set too far apart, letting the defender recover between them.
The shooter slowing down after the first screen.
Screeners moving or leaning — two moving screens is two turnovers.
gameSituations: Freeing a shooter when single pin downs aren't working.
ATO plays where you need a guaranteed clean look.
Against aggressive man defense that fights through single screens well.
